payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Standing on Her Work

¶1 One Tuesday last October, a date-formatting library called tidyclock vanished from the public package registry, and by morning several thousand websites could no longer tell their users what day it was. Its sole maintainer, a retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor, had deleted it after a decade of unpaid work and one rude bug report too many. Desmond Alcock's new book, Nobody's Job, opens with that night, and it is the right place to begin. I spent nine years maintaining a small text-parsing library used by companies I was never allowed to name, so I read Alcock with the uneasy attention of a patient reading her own chart.

¶2 The book's first half is a diagnosis, and it is a good one. Alcock surveyed four hundred of the most heavily downloaded packages in three programming languages and found that more than half depended on a single active volunteer. He calls these projects load-bearing walls that no inspector has visited, and the metaphor earns its keep: the walls are hidden inside the plaster of every bank, hospital, and school district that runs code on top of them. Nobody chose this arrangement. It accreted, one convenient download at a time, until the whole structure rested on the patience of people who could stop at any moment and owed us nothing if they did.

¶3 It is in the second half, where Alcock turns from diagnosis to cure, that the book loses its footing. His remedy is sponsorship: corporations that profit from open-source software should fund its maintainers, and he describes several foundations that already do so. I will grant that money has saved projects. A stipend kept at least one widely used encryption library alive after its maintainer nearly quit, and Alcock tells that story well. But a stipend changes what the work is. Consider the neighbor who shovels the shared walkway every winter because no one else will; the day you start paying her, the shoveling becomes a service, the snow becomes her problem, and you acquire the right to complain about ice. Sponsorship converts a gift into a contract, and the contract arrives written in the sponsor's priorities, not the project's.

¶4 I know something about how such gifts are received. In nine years I received roughly four thousand bug reports, most of them phrased as demands, several of them threatening, and one, from a hospital network in a city I have never visited, that began with the words "thank you." One. Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them at eleven at night? Alcock understands this loneliness better than any writer I have read, which is precisely why his faith in a check is so puzzling.

¶5 The better cure is already visible in the margins of his own book, though he never names it. The institutions that depend on these libraries do not lack money; they lack a sense that the maintenance is theirs to do. A regional bank runs tidyclock on its login page, employs ninety engineers, and has never assigned one of them a Friday afternoon to review tidyclock's open issues. Volunteer fire departments survive not because the town mails a check to the one person who owns a hose but because the people whose houses would burn show up for the drills. The obligation should attach to dependence, not to profit, and it should be paid in hours, not dollars. This will not rescue every project, and the smallest libraries will still rely on the stubbornness of individuals; but it would spread the weight across the walls that bear it.

¶6 Nobody's Job deserves the wide readership it will probably get. Read it for the first half, which will frighten you in the right way, and argue with the second, which will comfort you in the wrong one. The retired schoolteacher in Pell Harbor did not need a sponsor. She needed the several thousand of us who were standing on her work to notice that we were.

provenance.note: Original review essay of a fictional book, Nobody's Job, by the fictional author Desmond Alcock. All people, institutions, libraries and figures are invented.

blueprint.speaker: Imogen Tarrow, a former volunteer maintainer of a small text-parsing library for nine years, now writing criticism for a general-interest quarterly
blueprint.audience: Educated general readers of a literary and ideas quarterly, most of whom use software built on volunteer-maintained libraries without knowing it, including managers and engineers at the institutions that depend on such code
blueprint.exigence: The publication of Desmond Alcock's book Nobody's Job, which opens with the recent collapse of thousands of websites after the lone maintainer of the tidyclock library deleted it
blueprint.purpose: To recommend the book's diagnosis of fragile volunteer infrastructure while rejecting its prescribed cure of corporate sponsorship, and to propose instead that dependent institutions contribute maintenance labor
blueprint.context: A review essay in The Harrowgate Quarterly, written shortly after a widely noticed outage caused by a single volunteer quitting
blueprint.claim: Alcock is right that critical software rests on unseen, unpaid individuals, but wrong that money is the remedy; the obligation to maintain should attach to dependence and be paid in hours by the institutions that rely on the code.
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 opens with the tidyclock anecdote and establishes the reviewer's ethos as a former maintainer. Paragraph 4 shifts to personal testimony about ungrateful bug reports to show that the real deficit is recognition, not cash, and links that back to the critique. Paragraph 5 supplies the alternative cure (institutions lending hours, volunteer fire department analogy) with a qualification of its limits. Paragraph 6 renders the verdict and returns to the schoolteacher of the opening.

ALTON original passage
Proposal to Keep Brindle Creek Park Free

[1] Parks are something that most people have an opinion about. [2] Last month the Halvering Parks Commission announced that it is considering a 3-dollar entry fee at Brindle Creek Park to cover a 41,000-dollar maintenance shortfall. [3] As treasurer of the Halvering High student council, I am writing on behalf of our 38 members to ask the commission to vote against the fee at its May meeting. [4] Free parks are good for Halvering in a lot of ways.

[5] First, the fee would raise less money than it appears to. [6] Our council surveyed 212 students and parents outside the park gate on two Saturdays in April. [7] Sixty-four percent said they would visit less often if the fee were adopted, and 29 percent said they would stop coming altogether. [8] Fewer visitors would also mean fewer customers on Kettle Street, where the owner of Marron's Bakery told us that weekend park traffic brings in roughly a third of her sales. [9] The commission's projection counts on 60,000 paid entries a year, but that figure assumes attendance stays flat.

[10] Second, a free park can be cheaper to maintain than the commission's numbers suggest. [11] Our council already organizes a fall cleanup that drew 90 volunteers last October. [12] We propose expanding it into a monthly Saturday crew, supervised by parks staff, that handles litter pickup, mulching, and repainting the picnic shelters. [13] The commission's own report prices those three tasks at 17,000 dollars a year in contractor costs. [14] Students love being outside, so they will definitely show up. [15] Turning down that much free labor would be a pretty dumb move.

[16] Brindle Creek Park is where the cross-country team trains, where the kindergarten classes count ducks, and where my grandfather plays chess on Thursdays. [17] We ask the commission to keep the gate open and to let us help pay for it with our Saturdays. [18] Thank you for considering this proposal.

ALTON original passage
The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report

[1] Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot. [2] Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore. [3] This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened. [4] I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.

[5] The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting. [6] Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left. [7] Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon. [8] By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required. [9] Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.

[10] The members learned a great deal from the season. [11] Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day. [12] Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.

[13] Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration. [14] The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it. [15] We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

ALTON original passage

———

Source A
Four Towns Weigh One Library
Marisol Quent, The Valley Ledger, 2025

The Harlow Valley Council of Governments will vote in November on a plan to close the public library branches in Pennick, Oskar Bend, Lowen Mill and Dreyfield and replace them with a single regional hub on the former cannery lot in Pennick. The four branches together cost about 1.9 million dollars a year to run and recorded roughly 177,000 visits last year. Planners estimate the hub would cost 1.6 million dollars a year to operate and draw about 140,000 visits in its first full year, a figure they expect to climb once residents adjust. Construction is budgeted at 11 million dollars, with 4 million dollars coming from a state grant that lapses if the towns do not commit by spring. The hub would be open seven days and sixty-six hours a week; the current branches range from twenty hours a week in Dreyfield to forty-eight in Pennick. It would include a recording studio, a dedicated teen floor and a staffed homework center.

"We are not closing libraries, we are finally building one that can do what people keep asking us for," said council chair Ruthanne Bexley. Opponents point to distance. Dreyfield sits fourteen miles from the cannery lot, Lowen Mill nine and Oskar Bend six, and no public bus currently connects the four towns. Lowen Mill's representative, Tobias Enright, said he would not support the plan without "a written, funded answer for the people who walk to the library today." A council survey of 1,240 residents found that willingness to use the hub was highest in Pennick and fell steadily with distance.

———

Source B
Nostalgia Is Not a Library Budget
Desmond Kavale, retired branch director, The Harlow Valley Courier, 2025

I ran the Oskar Bend branch for nineteen years, and I loved it, so understand that I say this with no pleasure: the four-branch system is already a hub-and-nothing system. Pennick has the new books, the evening hours and the only children's librarian in the valley. The other three branches have what Pennick had eight years ago. When a Dreyfield teenager needs a quiet place to take an online exam, she borrows a car and drives to Pennick, because Dreyfield's building has two outlets and closes at four. We have been asking small towns to be loyal to buildings that cannot serve them.

Look at what it costs to open the doors. Every visit to Dreyfield costs the taxpayers 21.50 dollars; every visit to Pennick costs 7.50. That gap is not because Dreyfield's staff are careless. It is because a roof, a furnace, a security system and a desk clerk cost the same whether sixteen thousand people walk in or ninety-six thousand. Consolidating would free roughly 300,000 dollars a year, enough to hire three full-time specialists instead of four part-time generalists who rotate between buildings.

Yes, distance matters. But the honest comparison is not between a hub and four thriving branches. It is between a hub and four branches that are quietly rationing hours, materials and staff, and will ration more every year the furnaces age. A valley of eighteen thousand people can support one excellent library. It is proving, year by year, that it cannot support four adequate ones.

———

Source C
What Walks In at Three-Fifteen
Ilse Marrow, Dreyfield Town Newsletter, 2025

At three-fifteen the Dreyfield library fills the way a bus does. Eleven or twelve kids from the middle school come in with their backpacks half unzipped, and Mrs. Pell, who has worked the desk since before some of their parents were born, does not look up from her stamping until she has counted them. Then come the two retired men who read the paper on the bench by the window, and after them the woman from the apartments across the road who uses the one public computer to fill out her forms, because she has no computer and no car.

I have asked the council what these people are supposed to do on the day the doors close. I am told there may be a shuttle. A shuttle is a schedule, and a schedule is a reason not to go. A library you can walk to at three-fifteen is a different thing from a library you can be driven to on Saturdays.

The hub will be beautiful. I have seen the drawings, the teen floor and the recording studio, and I do not doubt that somebody in Pennick will use them. But the council survey put it plainly: only fourteen in a hundred Dreyfield residents expect to visit the hub as often as monthly. Thirty-three in a hundred visit our branch that often now. You cannot call that a service improvement. You can call it a service relocated to people who already have one. If the valley has 300,000 dollars a year to find, let it find it somewhere that does not take the only public room in this town.

———

Source D
Memorandum: Service Conditions for a Regional Library Hub
Office of Shared Services, Harlow Valley Council of Governments, 2025

This office was asked whether the proposed hub can be recommended as presented. Our answer is that it can be recommended only with three conditions attached, each funded in the same resolution that approves construction.

First, a fixed-route shuttle linking Dreyfield, Lowen Mill and Oskar Bend to the hub on at least four days a week, including one weekend day, at an estimated 95,000 dollars a year. Second, a staffed reading room of no fewer than twenty hours a week in Dreyfield and in Lowen Mill, housed in existing municipal buildings, with a public computer, holds pickup and a children's shelf, at an estimated 85,000 dollars a year for both. Third, a review after three years in which the hub's visit count is compared against the 140,000 projection, with the shuttle and reading rooms extended automatically if use from the outlying towns has not recovered to current levels.

These conditions reduce the projected annual saving from about 300,000 dollars to about 120,000 dollars. We consider that reduction the price of a plan that does not simply move service from the towns with the fewest alternatives to the town with the most. Without the conditions, the survey data suggest the hub would be used mainly by Pennick residents, and the valley would have spent 11 million dollars to serve roughly the people the Pennick branch already serves. With them, the hub becomes a genuine upgrade for every town rather than a consolidation that wears the name of one.

———

Source E (table)

Harlow Valley Council of Governments resident survey, 2025

Results from the Harlow Valley Council of Governments resident survey of 1,240 adults, conducted by mail and online in the spring of 2025. Figures are the percentage of respondents in each town.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
Many small towns share services such as fire protection, trash collection and school districts. Some are now asking whether public libraries should be shared the same way. In the fictional Harlow Valley, four towns are deciding whether to close their four small branch libraries and build one regional hub with longer hours, more staff and more equipment, located in the largest town. Supporters say one well-funded library serves everyone better than four underfunded ones. Opponents say a library people cannot walk to is not the same service in a new building. Others argue that consolidation can work only if it is paired with transportation and some form of local presence.

Carefully read the six sources that follow, including the introductory information for each source. Then write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether a group of small towns should replace several small public libraries with one shared regional hub.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that takes a defensible position on the question, which may be unconditional, conditional, or limited to particular circumstances.
- Select and use evidence from at least three of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning, and indicate clearly which sources you are using by citing them as Source A, Source B, and so on, or by the author's name.
- Explain how the evidence supports your reasoning; do not simply summarize or list what the sources say.
- You may use the sources to support, complicate, or argue against your own position, and you may draw on your own knowledge and experience in addition to the sources.
parts.model_answer:
When people argue about the Harlow Valley libraries, they usually talk as if the only question is money versus memory. The sources show something more uncomfortable: consolidation does not get rid of a cost, it moves it. The four towns should build the regional hub, but only if they fund Source D's shuttle and reading rooms in the same vote. Without those, the "savings" just get paid by the residents of Dreyfield and Lowen Mill in miles instead of by taxpayers in dollars.

The case for the hub is real, and Desmond Kavale makes it better than anyone because he actually ran one of the branches. His point is that the current system is already unequal. Pennick has "the only children's librarian in the valley," while Dreyfield's building "has two outlets and closes at four" (Source B). Source A backs this up: Dreyfield is open twenty hours a week, and the hub would be open sixty-six. A teenager who has to borrow a car to take an online exam in Pennick is not being served by her local branch. So opponents who picture four thriving libraries are defending something that doesn't exist.

But Kavale's best number is also misleading. He says each Dreyfield visit costs 21.50 dollars and each Pennick visit costs 7.50, dollars and Source F charts the hub at 11.40. dollars That looks like an obvious win until you do the math for the whole system. The four branches cost 1.9 million dollars for 177,000 visits (Source A), which comes to about 10.73 dollars a visit. That is actually cheaper than the hub. The hub saves money overall only because it expects 37,000 fewer visits. In other words, part of the "efficiency" is just fewer people using the library.

Who are those missing people? Source E answers that. In Dreyfield, 33 percent of residents visit their branch monthly, but only 14 percent expect to visit the hub that often, and 18 percent of households there have no car. Meanwhile Pennick's number goes up, from 41 to 44. Ilse Marrow's scene at three-fifteen puts faces on these percentages: the middle schoolers, the retired men, and the woman with "no computer and no car" who fills out forms on the one public computer (Source C). Kavale and Marrow aren't really disagreeing about facts. Kavale measures cost per visit, and Marrow measures who can get in the door. Divide dollars by visits and the number always looks better once the hardest people to serve stop showing up.

This is why Source D's conditions are not a watered-down compromise but the actual plan. The shuttle (95,000 dollars) and reading rooms (85,000 dollars) shrink the savings from 300,000 to 120,000, but they keep a public computer and a children's shelf within walking distance of Marrow's kids while also giving them a ride to a homework center their town could never afford. Marrow is right that "a schedule is a reason not to go," which is why the reading room matters more than the shuttle. It keeps the walk-in version of the library alive. Someone could say this is just a smaller copy of the four-branch system. Sample response, middle score (5/6; Thesis 1, Evidence and commentary 4, Sophistication 0):
The four towns of Harlow Valley should build the regional hub, but only if they also pay for a shuttle and keep small reading rooms open in the towns that lose their branches. Without those two things the hub would help Pennick and leave the other towns worse off than they are now.

The best argument for the hub is the one Desmond Kavale makes in Source B. He points out that the four branches are already unequal, since Pennick has the new books, the evening hours and the only children's librarian. Source F backs him up with numbers, because a visit to the Dreyfield branch costs 21.50 dollars and a visit to Pennick costs 7.50. The hub is projected to cost 11.40 per visit, which is a lot less than Dreyfield or Lowen Mill. Kavale also says that closing the branches would free up about 300,000 dollars a year for specialists. This shows that keeping four small buildings open means paying for roofs and furnaces instead of for staff and services, so the hub would be a better use of money for the valley.

However, cost per visit does not tell the whole story. If you take the whole system, 1.9 million dollars divided by 177,000 visits is about 10.70 per visit, which is actually less than the hub's projected 11.40. So the hub is not clearly cheaper per visit, and its savings come mostly from having fewer buildings. More important, the people who would lose the most are the ones with the fewest options. Source E shows that only 14 percent of Dreyfield residents expect to use the hub monthly, while 33 percent use their branch that often now, and 18 percent of Dreyfield households have no car. Ilse Marrow in Source C puts a face on those numbers with the woman from the apartments who uses the one public computer because she has no car. Marrow says a shuttle is "a schedule, and a schedule is a reason not to go," and that is a fair point, since Dreyfield is fourteen miles from the hub according to Source A.

That is why I think Source D has the right answer. The Office of Shared Services does not reject the hub, it says the hub can be recommended with three funded conditions, a shuttle, staffed reading rooms in Dreyfield and Lowen Mill, and a review after three years. These conditions cut the savings from 300,000 to about 120,000 dollars, but that is the price of making the hub serve everyone and not just Pennick. Marrow is right that a shuttle is not the same as a walk, but the reading rooms give people a place in town, which answers her concern better than a shuttle alone could.

In the end, the question is not only about money. Consolidation saves the taxpayers money, but it moves the cost onto people who have to travel, and that is only fair if the towns pay to reduce that burden. The hub with the conditions is worth building, and the hub without them is not.

It supports the thesis, but the essay does not look at whether 'expect' is only an intention.
   - "the woman from the apartments who uses the one public computer because she has no car" - Connects Marrow's example to the Source E car-ownership figure, but the explanation is brief and a little repetitive.

Libraries are an important part of any town and the people of Harlow Valley have a hard choice to make. sources.title: Four Towns Weigh One Library
sources.body:
The Harlow Valley Council of Governments will vote in November on a plan to close the public library branches in Pennick, Oskar Bend, Lowen Mill and Dreyfield and replace them with a single regional hub on the former cannery lot in Pennick. The four branches together cost about 1.9 million dollars a year to run and recorded roughly 177,000 visits last year. Planners estimate the hub would cost 1.6 million dollars a year to operate and draw about 140,000 visits in its first full year, a figure they expect to climb once residents adjust. Construction is budgeted at 11 million dollars, with 4 million dollars coming from a state grant that lapses if the towns do not commit by spring. The hub would be open seven days and sixty-six hours a week; the current branches range from twenty hours a week in Dreyfield to forty-eight in Pennick. It would include a recording studio, a dedicated teen floor and a staffed homework center.

"We are not closing libraries, we are finally building one that can do what people keep asking us for," said council chair Ruthanne Bexley. Opponents point to distance. Dreyfield sits fourteen miles from the cannery lot, Lowen Mill nine and Oskar Bend six, and no public bus currently connects the four towns. Lowen Mill's representative, Tobias Enright, said he would not support the plan without "a written, funded answer for the people who walk to the library today." A council survey of 1,240 residents found that willingness to use the hub was highest in Pennick and fell steadily with distance.

sources.title: Nostalgia Is Not a Library Budget
sources.attribution: Desmond Kavale, retired branch director, The Harlow Valley Courier, 2025
sources.body:
I ran the Oskar Bend branch for nineteen years, and I loved it, so understand that I say this with no pleasure: the four-branch system is already a hub-and-nothing system. Pennick has the new books, the evening hours and the only children's librarian in the valley. The other three branches have what Pennick had eight years ago. When a Dreyfield teenager needs a quiet place to take an online exam, she borrows a car and drives to Pennick, because Dreyfield's building has two outlets and closes at four. We have been asking small towns to be loyal to buildings that cannot serve them.

Look at what it costs to open the doors. Every visit to Dreyfield costs the taxpayers 21.50 dollars; every visit to Pennick costs 7.50. That gap is not because Dreyfield's staff are careless. It is because a roof, a furnace, a security system and a desk clerk cost the same whether sixteen thousand people walk in or ninety-six thousand. Consolidating would free roughly 300,000 dollars a year, enough to hire three full-time specialists instead of four part-time generalists who rotate between buildings.

Yes, distance matters. But the honest comparison is not between a hub and four thriving branches. It is between a hub and four branches that are quietly rationing hours, materials and staff, and will ration more every year the furnaces age. A valley of eighteen thousand people can support one excellent library. It is proving, year by year, that it cannot support four adequate ones.

sources.title: What Walks In at Three-Fifteen
sources.body:
At three-fifteen the Dreyfield library fills the way a bus does. Eleven or twelve kids from the middle school come in with their backpacks half unzipped, and Mrs. Pell, who has worked the desk since before some of their parents were born, does not look up from her stamping until she has counted them. Then come the two retired men who read the paper on the bench by the window, and after them the woman from the apartments across the road who uses the one public computer to fill out her forms, because she has no computer and no car.

I have asked the council what these people are supposed to do on the day the doors close. I am told there may be a shuttle. A shuttle is a schedule, and a schedule is a reason not to go. A library you can walk to at three-fifteen is a different thing from a library you can be driven to on Saturdays.

The hub will be beautiful. I have seen the drawings, the teen floor and the recording studio, and I do not doubt that somebody in Pennick will use them. But the council survey put it plainly: only fourteen in a hundred Dreyfield residents expect to visit the hub as often as monthly. Thirty-three in a hundred visit our branch that often now. You cannot call that a service improvement. You can call it a service relocated to people who already have one. If the valley has 300,000 dollars a year to find, let it find it somewhere that does not take the only public room in this town.

This office was asked whether the proposed hub can be recommended as presented. Our answer is that it can be recommended only with three conditions attached, each funded in the same resolution that approves construction.

First, a fixed-route shuttle linking Dreyfield, Lowen Mill and Oskar Bend to the hub on at least four days a week, including one weekend day, at an estimated 95,000 dollars a year. Second, a staffed reading room of no fewer than twenty hours a week in Dreyfield and in Lowen Mill, housed in existing municipal buildings, with a public computer, holds pickup and a children's shelf, at an estimated 85,000 dollars a year for both. Third, a review after three years in which the hub's visit count is compared against the 140,000 projection, with the shuttle and reading rooms extended automatically if use from the outlying towns has not recovered to current levels.

These conditions reduce the projected annual saving from about 300,000 dollars to about 120,000 dollars. We consider that reduction the price of a plan that does not simply move service from the towns with the fewest alternatives to the town with the most. Without the conditions, the survey data suggest the hub would be used mainly by Pennick residents, and the valley would have spent 11 million dollars to serve roughly the people the Pennick branch already serves. With them, the hub becomes a genuine upgrade for every town rather than a consolidation that wears the name of one.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt, only summarizes what the sources say, or states that the question has two sides without choosing one. Statements like 'There are many factors a town should consider before closing libraries' earn 0.
descriptors.1: A thesis that takes a defensible position on whether small towns should replace several small libraries with one regional hub. The position may be a flat yes or no, a conditional yes (only with transit and local reading rooms, for example), or a limited position (hub for towns within a short distance but not for distant ones). The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.

rows.task_specific: A conditional position counts as defensible only if it names the condition. 'Towns should consolidate only if they fund a way for people without cars to reach the hub' earns the point; 'Towns should consolidate if it makes sense for them' does not. A thesis that picks a stance but mislabels it (calling Source D an opponent, for instance) still earns the point; source accuracy is scored in Row B.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, offers no evidence from the sources, or uses evidence from fewer than two sources with no connection to any claim.
descriptors.1: Uses evidence from at least two sources but mostly summarizes them in turn ('Source A says... Source B says...') with little or no explanation of how the evidence supports a position. Commentary, where present, repeats the evidence in other words.
descriptors.2: Uses evidence from at least three sources and connects at least some of it to the thesis, but the reasoning is thin or uneven: the essay may lean on one source and mention the others briefly, make general claims ('distance is a big problem') without pointing to the specific figures or examples that show it, or leave the reader to infer why a cited fact matters.
descriptors.3: Uses specific evidence from at least three sources to support a line of reasoning, and explains for most of that evidence how it supports the claim. The essay usually points to a particular figure, example or quotation (the 14 percent expected hub use in Dreyfield, the 21.50 dollar cost per visit, Marrow's three-fifteen scene) and says what it shows. Some commentary may still be generic or some evidence may be dropped in without explanation.
descriptors.4: Uses specific, well-chosen evidence from at least three sources, consistently explains how each piece supports the line of reasoning, and builds the paragraphs into a developed argument rather than a list. The essay engages with evidence that complicates its position (for example, a pro-hub essay that confronts the survey drop-off in Source E, or an anti-hub essay that confronts the hours and staffing gap in Sources A and B) and explains why its position still holds.

rows.task_specific: Sources A, E and F are informational and can support any stance; using them does not by itself show synthesis unless the essay explains what the number means for its argument. Counting the number of sources cited is not enough for 3 or 4: an essay that cites five sources in one sentence each with no commentary stays at 2. Correct arithmetic drawn from the sources (for example, that the current system's overall cost per visit, 1.9 million dollars over 177,000 visits, is actually lower than the hub's projected 11.40) counts as strong evidence use. Misreading a source in a way that reverses its meaning (claiming Source D opposes the hub outright, or that Source E shows Dreyfield residents rarely use their branch) caps the row at 2 unless the misreading is minor and isolated.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: The argument is straightforward and does not complicate its own claims, treats the issue as a simple contest between savings and sentiment, or relies on sweeping statements and ornamental prose instead of precise thought. Merely mentioning 'the other side' before dismissing it does not earn the point.
descriptors.1: The essay does at least one of the following in a sustained way, not in a single sentence: explains why the tension exists (for example, that per-visit cost and per-person access measure different things, so Sources B and C are not actually disagreeing about facts); situates the argument in a wider context, such as what a public institution owes to the residents least able to travel; examines the limits of the evidence, such as noting that the hub visit projection is only a projection and the 'expect to visit' survey column records intention rather than behavior; or writes with a controlled, precise style that makes the reasoning clearer.

rows.task_specific: A strong candidate for this point is an essay that identifies that consolidation shifts who bears the cost (from taxpayers in dollars to outlying residents in distance) and argues from that insight. Another is an essay that uses Source D's conditions to test whether a 'both' solution is really a compromise or simply a smaller version of the status quo. Vocabulary alone, a vivid opening, or a closing call to 'remember what libraries are for' does not earn the point.

scoring_notes: Score the three rows independently; an essay can earn Row C without earning a 4 in Row B, and vice versa.
Essays that cite the sources by author name (Kavale, Marrow) instead of letter are acceptable.
An essay that uses only two sources cannot score above 1 in Row B regardless of quality.

Numbers in the sources are consistent with one another; an essay that notices and uses a relationship between two sources (Source B's cost figures with Source F, Source C's percentages with Source E) is doing synthesis and should be credited for it.
Do not penalize an essay for taking a position the grader finds unpersuasive; penalize only unsupported or self-contradicting reasoning.
Personal experience with a local library counts as evidence only when it is tied to the argument; it does not substitute for the three-source minimum.

common_pitfalls: Summarizing each source in turn without connecting the summaries to a claim.
Treating the issue as money versus feelings, when Sources E and F show that both sides have numbers and the dispute is about which numbers matter.
Misreading Source D as opposition; it supports the hub under conditions, which makes it the most useful source for a middle position.
Citing the 300,000 dollar saving without noticing that Source D shows it falls to 120,000 once access conditions are funded.

Using the cost-per-visit chart to claim the hub is cheaper per visit than the current system; the hub's projected 11.40 is lower than three branches but higher than Pennick and higher than the system's combined average.
Reading the survey's 'expect to visit the hub' column as a measure of what residents will actually do rather than what they predict.
Quoting Marrow's scene at length as decoration without explaining what it demonstrates about who uses a walkable branch.
Writing a thesis that lists considerations rather than taking a position.
Ignoring the state grant deadline in Source A, which is the reason the choice cannot simply be postponed, and so missing a chance to address urgency.

samples.essay:
When people argue about the Harlow Valley libraries, they usually talk as if the only question is money versus memory. The sources show something more uncomfortable: consolidation does not get rid of a cost, it moves it. The four towns should build the regional hub, but only if they fund Source D's shuttle and reading rooms in the same vote. Without those, the "savings" just get paid by the residents of Dreyfield and Lowen Mill in miles instead of by taxpayers in dollars.

The case for the hub is real, and Desmond Kavale makes it better than anyone because he actually ran one of the branches. His point is that the current system is already unequal. Pennick has "the only children's librarian in the valley," while Dreyfield's building "has two outlets and closes at four" (Source B). Source A backs this up: Dreyfield is open twenty hours a week, and the hub would be open sixty-six. A teenager who has to borrow a car to take an online exam in Pennick is not being served by her local branch. So opponents who picture four thriving libraries are defending something that doesn't exist.

But Kavale's best number is also misleading. He says each Dreyfield visit costs 21.50 dollars and each Pennick visit costs 7.50, dollars and Source F charts the hub at 11.40. dollars That looks like an obvious win until you do the math for the whole system. The four branches cost 1.9 million dollars for 177,000 visits (Source A), which comes to about 10.73 dollars a visit. That is actually cheaper than the hub. The hub saves money overall only because it expects 37,000 fewer visits. In other words, part of the "efficiency" is just fewer people using the library.

Who are those missing people? Source E answers that. In Dreyfield, 33 percent of residents visit their branch monthly, but only 14 percent expect to visit the hub that often, and 18 percent of households there have no car. Meanwhile Pennick's number goes up, from 41 to 44. Ilse Marrow's scene at three-fifteen puts faces on these percentages: the middle schoolers, the retired men, and the woman with "no computer and no car" who fills out forms on the one public computer (Source C). Kavale and Marrow aren't really disagreeing about facts. Kavale measures cost per visit, and Marrow measures who can get in the door. Divide dollars by visits and the number always looks better once the hardest people to serve stop showing up.

This is why Source D's conditions are not a watered-down compromise but the actual plan. The shuttle (95,000 dollars) and reading rooms (85,000 dollars) shrink the savings from 300,000 to 120,000, but they keep a public computer and a children's shelf within walking distance of Marrow's kids while also giving them a ride to a homework center their town could never afford. Marrow is right that "a schedule is a reason not to go," which is why the reading room matters more than the shuttle. It keeps the walk-in version of the library alive. Someone could say this is just a smaller copy of the four-branch system. It isn't, though, because a twenty-hour room in a town hall doesn't need its own roof and furnace, and those are exactly the costs Kavale blames.

The review matters too, because so much of the case rests on guesses. The 140,000 visits is a projection, and "expect to visit" in Source E records what people wrote on a survey, not what they will do. A plan built on predictions should come with a promise to check them, and Source D's automatic extension makes that promise binding instead of hopeful.

The grant deadline makes it tempting to vote yes and work out the details later. The valley should vote yes, but only on the version where the details are paid for up front. Otherwise the towns with the fewest alternatives end up paying for a library they mostly can't reach.

The four towns of Harlow Valley should build the regional hub, but only if they also pay for a shuttle and keep small reading rooms open in the towns that lose their branches. Without those two things the hub would help Pennick and leave the other towns worse off than they are now.

The best argument for the hub is the one Desmond Kavale makes in Source B. He points out that the four branches are already unequal, since Pennick has the new books, the evening hours and the only children's librarian. Source F backs him up with numbers, because a visit to the Dreyfield branch costs 21.50 dollars and a visit to Pennick costs 7.50. The hub is projected to cost 11.40 per visit, which is a lot less than Dreyfield or Lowen Mill. Kavale also says that closing the branches would free up about 300,000 dollars a year for specialists. This shows that keeping four small buildings open means paying for roofs and furnaces instead of for staff and services, so the hub would be a better use of money for the valley.

However, cost per visit does not tell the whole story. If you take the whole system, 1.9 million dollars divided by 177,000 visits is about 10.70 per visit, which is actually less than the hub's projected 11.40. So the hub is not clearly cheaper per visit, and its savings come mostly from having fewer buildings. More important, the people who would lose the most are the ones with the fewest options. Source E shows that only 14 percent of Dreyfield residents expect to use the hub monthly, while 33 percent use their branch that often now, and 18 percent of Dreyfield households have no car. Ilse Marrow in Source C puts a face on those numbers with the woman from the apartments who uses the one public computer because she has no car. Marrow says a shuttle is "a schedule, and a schedule is a reason not to go," and that is a fair point, since Dreyfield is fourteen miles from the hub according to Source A.

That is why I think Source D has the right answer. The Office of Shared Services does not reject the hub, it says the hub can be recommended with three funded conditions, a shuttle, staffed reading rooms in Dreyfield and Lowen Mill, and a review after three years. These conditions cut the savings from 300,000 to about 120,000 dollars, but that is the price of making the hub serve everyone and not just Pennick. Marrow is right that a shuttle is not the same as a walk, but the reading rooms give people a place in town, which answers her concern better than a shuttle alone could.

In the end, the question is not only about money. Consolidation saves the taxpayers money, but it moves the cost onto people who have to travel, and that is only fair if the towns pay to reduce that burden. The hub with the conditions is worth building, and the hub without them is not.

Libraries are an important part of any town and the people of Harlow Valley have a hard choice to make. There are good points on both sides of whether to build one regional hub or keep the four small libraries. In my opinion the towns should think carefully about what is best for everyone before they decide.

Source B says that the old system is not working very well. The writer ran the Oskar Bend branch for nineteen years and says that Dreyfield's building has only two outlets and closes at four. He also says it costs 21.50 dollars per visit in Dreyfield and only 7.50 in Pennick. This shows that the small libraries are expensive and the hub would save money. Source F also shows the costs, with the hub at 11.40 which is in the middle.

On the other hand Source C is about Dreyfield and it describes kids coming in at three-fifteen and a woman who has no car. The writer says a shuttle is a schedule and a schedule is a reason not to go. This is a good point because lots of people would not be able to get to the hub. Source E has a table that shows the percent of people who would use the hub is lower in Dreyfield, 14 percent, than in Pennick. So distance is a big problem for the hub.

Source D is a memo that says the hub can be recommended but only with conditions like a shuttle and reading rooms. This is a kind of middle option and it costs some money but the saving is still there.

Overall both sides have a point. The hub has longer hours and more staff but people far away might lose out. The towns should look at all of this and make the best choice for the valley.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Remarks on the North Wharf Rezoning
Marguerite Osgood, retired harbor pilot, remarks delivered at a Tillet's Reach town meeting on the north wharf rezoning proposal, 2019

¶1 (1) For thirty-one years I climbed a rope ladder up the side of other people's ships. (2) My job was simple to describe and hard to do: bring the ship through the channel, past shoals that have sunk boats since before this town had a name, and lay it against the pier without breaking anything. (3) I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. (4) I am a woman who knows where the rocks are.

¶2 (5) The proposal before you would rezone the north wharf for what the brochure calls a residential marina village. (6) I have read the brochure. (7) It is handsome. (8) The renderings show cafes with striped awnings, a boardwalk, furled sailboats, and not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot. (9) That absence is the point of the drawing, and it ought to be the point of our discussion.

¶3 (10) Let me be fair to the people who drew it. (11) The fishing fleet is smaller than it was. (12) The ice house closed in 2011, the fuel dock loses money three months a year, and condominium taxes are real money for a town that cannot fix the culvert on Pell Street. (13) If I told you the working wharf is a gold mine, you would be right to laugh me out of the room. (14) It is not a gold mine. (15) It is a kitchen.

¶4 (16) A kitchen does not make money by itself, but try running a restaurant without one. (17) The diesel mechanic, the welder, the woman who patches nets behind the co-op, the boatyards, the supply store where half of you buy your winter boots: they are all here because the boats are here. (18) Take away the place where a boat can tie up, unload, refuel, and haul out, and the boats go to Carrow Point. (19) Then the mechanic goes. (20) Then the welder. (21) Then the kids who might have learned a trade from either of them go somewhere that still has trades to learn. (22) Last year the co-op landed just under four million dollars of catch across that wharf, and the harbor master counts about one hundred and forty jobs that touch it directly. (23) In a town of six thousand, that is the difference between a place that works and a place that is merely looked at.

¶5 (24) I want to say something now that is harder to put in a brochure. (25) On a February morning in 1994 the trawler Anna Belle lost her engine in the outer channel with a gale building from the northeast. (26) The men who went out after her were not the rescue crew at Harrow Light, forty minutes away, but Dale Cuttery in his lobster boat and two deckhands who had been drinking coffee at the fuel dock. (27) They were there in eleven minutes because they were already there. (28) A marina full of shrink-wrapped sailboats does not go out in a gale. (29) It cannot. (30) Nobody is aboard.

¶6 (31) So what are we really deciding? (32) Not whether Tillet's Reach will have a waterfront; it will have one either way. (33) We are deciding whether the waterfront belongs to the town or merely faces it. (34) A working harbor is loud, it smells of bait and diesel, and it will never photograph as well as a boardwalk. (35) But it answers back. (36) It sends out boats, it brings home fish, it teaches sixteen-year-olds to splice a line and read a falling tide. (37) The pretty version does none of those things; it only asks that we admire it.

¶7 (38) I have brought a great many ships safely in. (39) I would like, before I am finished, to help bring one town in too. (40) Keep the north wharf working. (41) Vote no on the rezoning, and then let us sit down and find another way to pay for the culvert.

parts.prompt:
Speaker: Marguerite Osgood, a harbor pilot who retired after thirty-one years guiding ships into the port of Tillet's Reach, a fictional coastal town of about six thousand people. Audience: residents and elected council members gathered at a town meeting in 2019. Exigence: the council is about to vote on a developer's proposal to rezone the north wharf, the town's last commercial working pier, for a residential marina village of condominiums, cafes, and a recreational boat basin. Purpose: to persuade the town to reject the rezoning and preserve the working waterfront by reframing the wharf not as a failing business but as the infrastructure on which the town's trades, safety, and identity depend, while acknowledging the town's real financial pressures.

Marguerite Osgood spent thirty-one years as a harbor pilot, boarding arriving ships and guiding them through the channel into the port of Tillet's Reach. In 2019, the town council prepared to vote on a proposal to rezone the north wharf, the town's last working commercial pier, for condominiums and a recreational marina. Osgood, by then retired, spoke at the public meeting held before the vote. The passage below is the text of her remarks. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Osgood makes to persuade the town to keep the north wharf a working waterfront.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the rhetorical choices Osgood makes and how they advance her purpose.
- Select and cite specific evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.
- Explain in your commentary how the evidence you have chosen demonstrates the way Osgood's choices work on her audience and serve her purpose.
parts.model_answer:
When Marguerite Osgood stood up at the Tillet's Reach town meeting, she was speaking to an audience that already knew the wharf was losing money. The developer's brochure had a simple pitch: pretty condos, tax revenue, and maybe a culvert that finally gets fixed. Osgood could not win by pretending those numbers away. Instead she builds her speech like one of her channel crossings, carefully and in order. First she earns trust as a practical insider who admits the wharf's weaknesses. Then she redefines the wharf from a failing business into infrastructure the town cannot function without. Finally she shifts the question from money to who is actually on the water when something goes wrong. By the end, a vote that looked like a budget decision feels like a decision about what kind of town Tillet's Reach wants to be.

Osgood opens by shrinking her own authority in a way that actually increases it. "I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. I am a woman who knows where the rocks are." prompt.scenario: Speaker: Marguerite Osgood, a harbor pilot who retired after thirty-one years guiding ships into the port of Tillet's Reach, a fictional coastal town of about six thousand people. Audience: residents and elected council members gathered at a town meeting in 2019. Exigence: the council is about to vote on a developer's proposal to rezone the north wharf, the town's last commercial working pier, for a residential marina village of condominiums, cafes, and a recreational boat basin. Purpose: to persuade the town to reject the rezoning and preserve the working waterfront by reframing the wharf not as a failing business but as the infrastructure on which the town's trades, safety, and identity depend, while acknowledging the town's real financial pressures.
prompt.task: Marguerite Osgood spent thirty-one years as a harbor pilot, boarding arriving ships and guiding them through the channel into the port of Tillet's Reach. In 2019, the town council prepared to vote on a proposal to rezone the north wharf, the town's last working commercial pier, for condominiums and a recreational marina. Osgood, by then retired, spoke at the public meeting held before the vote. The passage below is the text of her remarks. Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Osgood makes to persuade the town to keep the north wharf a working waterfront.

Select and cite specific evidence from the passage to support your line of reasoning.

sources.genre: public address at a town meeting
sources.body:
For thirty-one years I climbed a rope ladder up the side of other people's ships. My job was simple to describe and hard to do: bring the ship through the channel, past shoals that have sunk boats since before this town had a name, and lay it against the pier without breaking anything. I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. I am a woman who knows where the rocks are.

The proposal before you would rezone the north wharf for what the brochure calls a residential marina village. I have read the brochure. It is handsome. The renderings show cafes with striped awnings, a boardwalk, furled sailboats, and not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot. That absence is the point of the drawing, and it ought to be the point of our discussion.

Let me be fair to the people who drew it. The fishing fleet is smaller than it was. The ice house closed in 2011, the fuel dock loses money three months a year, and condominium taxes are real money for a town that cannot fix the culvert on Pell Street. If I told you the working wharf is a gold mine, you would be right to laugh me out of the room. It is not a gold mine. It is a kitchen.

A kitchen does not make money by itself, but try running a restaurant without one. The diesel mechanic, the welder, the woman who patches nets behind the co-op, the boatyards, the supply store where half of you buy your winter boots: they are all here because the boats are here. Take away the place where a boat can tie up, unload, refuel, and haul out, and the boats go to Carrow Point. Then the mechanic goes. Then the welder. Then the kids who might have learned a trade from either of them go somewhere that still has trades to learn. Last year the co-op landed just under four million dollars of catch across that wharf, and the harbor master counts about one hundred and forty jobs that touch it directly. In a town of six thousand, that is the difference between a place that works and a place that is merely looked at.

I want to say something now that is harder to put in a brochure. On a February morning in 1994 the trawler Anna Belle lost her engine in the outer channel with a gale building from the northeast. The men who went out after her were not the rescue crew at Harrow Light, forty minutes away, but Dale Cuttery in his lobster boat and two deckhands who had been drinking coffee at the fuel dock. They were there in eleven minutes because they were already there. A marina full of shrink-wrapped sailboats does not go out in a gale. It cannot. Nobody is aboard.

So what are we really deciding? Not whether Tillet's Reach will have a waterfront; it will have one either way. We are deciding whether the waterfront belongs to the town or merely faces it. A working harbor is loud, it smells of bait and diesel, and it will never photograph as well as a boardwalk. But it answers back. It sends out boats, it brings home fish, it teaches sixteen-year-olds to splice a line and read a falling tide. The pretty version does none of those things; it only asks that we admire it.

I have brought a great many ships safely in. I would like, before I am finished, to help bring one town in too. Keep the north wharf working. Vote no on the rezoning, and then let us sit down and find another way to pay for the culvert.

(16) A kitchen does not make money by itself, but try running a restaurant without one.

(17) The diesel mechanic, the welder, the woman who patches nets behind the co-op, the boatyards, the supply store where half of you buy your winter boots: they are all here because the boats are here.
(18) Take away the place where a boat can tie up, unload, refuel, and haul out, and the boats go to Carrow Point.
(19) Then the mechanic goes.
(20) Then the welder.
(21) Then the kids who might have learned a trade from either of them go somewhere that still has trades to learn.
(22) Last year the co-op landed just under four million dollars of catch across that wharf, and the harbor master counts about one hundred and forty jobs that touch it directly.
(23) In a town of six thousand, that is the difference between a place that works and a place that is merely looked at.
(24) I want to say something now that is harder to put in a brochure.
(25) On a February morning in 1994 the trawler Anna Belle lost her engine in the outer channel with a gale building from the northeast.
(26) The men who went out after her were not the rescue crew at Harrow Light, forty minutes away, but Dale Cuttery in his lobster boat and two deckhands who had been drinking coffee at the fuel dock.
(27) They were there in eleven minutes because they were already there.
(28) A marina full of shrink-wrapped sailboats does not go out in a gale.
(29) It cannot.
(30) Nobody is aboard.
(31) So what are we really deciding?
(32) Not whether Tillet's Reach will have a waterfront; it will have one either way.
(33) We are deciding whether the waterfront belongs to the town or merely faces it.
(34) A working harbor is loud, it smells of bait and diesel, and it will never photograph as well as a boardwalk.
(35) But it answers back.
(36) It sends out boats, it brings home fish, it teaches sixteen-year-olds to splice a line and read a falling tide.
(37) The pretty version does none of those things; it only asks that we admire it.
(38) I have brought a great many ships safely in.
(39) I would like, before I am finished, to help bring one town in too.
(40) Keep the north wharf working.
(41) Vote no on the rezoning, and then let us sit down and find another way to pay for the culvert.
sources.stance: opposes the rezoning; argues the working wharf is essential infrastructure for the town's trades, safety, and identity

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt (for example, 'Osgood uses many rhetorical choices to persuade the town'), or a statement that merely summarizes what Osgood says about the wharf without making a claim about how she persuades. A thesis that takes a position on whether the wharf should be rezoned, rather than on Osgood's rhetoric, also earns 0.
descriptors.1: A defensible claim about how Osgood's choices work toward her purpose. The claim may be modest (for example, that she establishes herself as a practical insider and then redefines the wharf as infrastructure rather than a business) but it must name a rhetorical move or strategy and connect it to persuading the town to keep the wharf working. The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.

rows.task_specific: Acceptable theses identify at least one specific choice or pattern (the kitchen metaphor, the concession in paragraph 3, the Anna Belle anecdote, the shift from economic to moral framing, the piloting metaphor that frames the whole speech) and link it to the goal of defeating the rezoning. A thesis that lists devices with no claim about effect ('Osgood uses metaphor, statistics, and a story') is on the line; award the point only if the essay's opening sentences attach those devices to a purpose.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, summarizes the speech, or offers evidence that is not from the passage.
descriptors.1: Mostly summary or paraphrase of Osgood's points about the wharf with little attention to how she says them. Evidence, if quoted, is general and commentary consists of labels ('this is pathos') with no explanation of effect on the town-meeting audience.
descriptors.2: Quotes or closely references specific moments and names the choices accurately, but commentary is thin or repetitive: it asserts that a choice 'makes the audience feel' or 'helps her argument' without explaining the mechanism. Typical 2 essays treat each device in isolation and do not connect them to the exigence (an imminent council vote on a developer's proposal).
descriptors.3: Specific evidence from several parts of the passage, with commentary that explains how at least two or three choices serve the purpose in ways tied to this audience and occasion. The essay has a line of reasoning, but one or more body paragraphs may slip into summary, or the analysis may be uneven (strong on the anecdote, generic on the opening ethos).
descriptors.4: Specific, well-chosen evidence from across the passage supports a sustained line of reasoning. Commentary consistently explains how choices function for this audience: for example, why the concession about the ice house and fuel dock makes the later kitchen metaphor credible, why the Anna Belle story is placed after the numbers rather than before, or how the closing piloting metaphor returns to the ethos of the opening. The essay shows how choices work together rather than as a checklist.

rows.task_specific: Choices that count as valid evidence include: the opening ethos and antithesis (sentences 1-4); the description of the brochure and the pointed absence (8-9); the concession and rebuttal (10-15); the kitchen metaphor and restaurant analogy (14-16); the enumeration of trades and the direct address 'half of you' (17); the cause-and-effect chain with 'Then' repetition and shrinking sentences (18-21); the statistics and their scaling to a town of six thousand (22-23); the tone shift and anecdote (24-30), including the short sentences 'It cannot. Nobody is aboard.'; the rhetorical question and redefinition of the decision (31-33); the personification 'it answers back' and the parallel verbs (35-36); the closing metaphor of bringing a town in (38-39) and the conciliatory offer about the culvert (41). Essays need not use these labels; what matters is accurate description of the move and explanation of its effect. Merely noting that Osgood 'uses numbers' is weak; noting that she volunteers the unflattering numbers first (12) so the favorable ones (22) land as honest counts for more.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Competent analysis that stays at the level of device plus effect, or an essay whose attempts at complexity are decorative (ornate vocabulary, sweeping claims about 'society') rather than analytical.
descriptors.1: The essay does one or more of the following convincingly and throughout rather than in a single sentence: explains how the structure of the speech works as a whole (the movement from credibility, to concession, to economics, to the rescue story, to redefinition, to the closing ask); examines tensions in Osgood's rhetoric, such as the risk that a retired pilot's nostalgia could read as self-interest and how she heads that off by conceding the fleet's decline and ending with an offer to solve the culvert problem; situates the speech in its rhetorical situation by considering what council members and residents who favor the tax revenue would need to hear; or writes with a consistently precise and controlled prose style.

rows.task_specific: A strong candidate for this point notices that Osgood never attacks the developers, that she borrows the brochure's own silence (no forklifts) as her strongest exhibit, or that the Anna Belle story quietly reframes the question from money to safety and who is physically present on the water. Do not award the point for simply using the word 'juxtaposition' or for an eloquent conclusion attached to an otherwise formulaic essay.

scoring_notes: Score holistically within each row; an essay that earns 4 in Row B will almost always also earn the thesis point, but check that the claim is about rhetoric, not about the merits of rezoning.

Students may describe the choices without technical names. 'She stacks three short sentences so the loss sounds like dominoes falling' is full-credit commentary on sentences 19-21 even without the word 'repetition'.
Essays that argue Osgood is wrong or right about the wharf are off task; score them only on whatever rhetorical analysis they contain.
An essay built on one well-analyzed section (for example, only paragraph 5) can reach a 3 in Row B if the commentary is rich, but reaching 4 requires evidence from more than one part of the speech.

Misreadings that distort the passage (for example, claiming Osgood opposes any change or that she dismisses the town's money problems) cap Row B at 2 because the commentary rests on a false account of the text.

defensible_positions: Osgood persuades by first establishing herself as a practical insider rather than an advocate, then conceding the wharf's financial weakness so that her redefinition of it as a kitchen, as infrastructure the whole town's economy sits on, is received as candor rather than special pleading.

The speech moves deliberately from logos (jobs, dollars, cause and effect) to pathos (the Anna Belle rescue) to a redefinition of the decision itself, so that by the final paragraph the vote is no longer about tax revenue but about whether the waterfront 'belongs to the town or merely faces it.'

Osgood turns the developer's own brochure against the proposal by reading its omissions, and she sustains that contrast between the pictured and the working harbor through the whole address, culminating in the personification of a harbor that 'answers back.'

The piloting metaphor frames the entire speech: Osgood opens as the person who knows where the rocks are and closes by offering to pilot the town itself, converting her professional ethos into moral authority for the vote.
lines_of_reasoning: Ethos to concession to metaphor: show how sentences 1-4 earn trust, sentences 10-13 spend some of it on honesty, and sentences 14-16 cash it in on the kitchen claim.
The economic argument as a chain: the enumeration in 17, the conditional in 18, the collapsing sentences in 19-21, and the scaled statistics in 22-23 together make loss feel sequential and local.
The tone shift at sentence 24 and why the anecdote follows rather than precedes the numbers; the effect of the three short sentences 28-30 on an audience that includes people who remember 1994.

The redefinition in 31-33 and the closing: how the rhetorical question lets Osgood replace the council's framing with her own, and how the final sentence's offer to solve the culvert problem removes the audience's main reason to vote yes.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Establishes Osgood as a practical expert with physical, earned knowledge of the harbor rather than a partisan, so her later claims about what the wharf does are heard as testimony.
Contrasts credentialed outsiders (planner, developer, economist) with local knowledge ('where the rocks are'), quietly positioning the brochure's authors as people who do not know the water.
Praises the brochure as 'handsome' and then exposes what it leaves out, turning the developer's own image into evidence that the proposal erases the working harbor.
Two clipped sentences followed by a long catalog slow the audience down before the reveal of the missing forklifts and crab pots.
Admits the fleet's decline and the town's money problems before anyone can raise them, protecting her credibility and setting up the pivot from 'gold mine' to 'kitchen'.
Reframes the wharf from a business judged by profit to infrastructure judged by what it enables, which is the central conceptual move of the speech.
The restaurant-without-a-kitchen comparison makes an abstract economic dependency instantly graspable to a general audience.

Anaphora on 'Then' with shrinking sentences mimics departures happening one after another.
Supplies concrete figures and then scales them to a town of six thousand so modest numbers register as decisive.
Signals a move from economics to something 'harder to put in a brochure,' preparing the audience for an emotional and moral appeal.
The 1994 rescue of the Anna Belle shows that a working harbor saves lives because its people are physically present, an argument no tax figure can answer.
Three abrupt sentences about empty shrink-wrapped boats evoke a harbor that looks after no one, turning the brochure's tidiness into a kind of abandonment.
Invites the audience to reconsider the terms of the vote and opens space for Osgood to redefine them.
Redefines the decision as a question of belonging versus facing, shifting the ground from revenue to identity.

source_uses.usable_for: All evidence must come from Osgood's remarks; the passage supplies ethos, concession, metaphor, logos, anecdote, tone shift, redefinition, and a framing metaphor that closes the loop.

common_pitfalls: Summarizing Osgood's argument about the wharf paragraph by paragraph instead of analyzing how the speech is built to persuade.
Labeling the Anna Belle story as 'pathos' and stopping there, without explaining why a rescue in which the rescuers were 'already there' answers the marina proposal specifically.
Treating the concession in paragraph 3 as a weakness or an inconsistency rather than as a deliberate credibility move that sets up the kitchen metaphor.
Ignoring the audience: forgetting that this is a town meeting before a council vote and that Osgood is speaking to neighbors, some of whom want the tax revenue.
Writing a thesis that takes a side on waterfront development rather than making a claim about rhetoric.
Listing six devices in a single paragraph with one quotation each and no line of reasoning connecting them.

Overlooking the frame: the opening claim 'I am a woman who knows where the rocks are' and the closing wish to 'bring one town in' are the same metaphor, and essays that miss the return miss the speech's structure.
Inventing effects not supported by the text, such as claiming Osgood shames or threatens the council, when her tone is measured and her final sentence is cooperative.

samples.essay:
When Marguerite Osgood stood up at the Tillet's Reach town meeting, she was speaking to an audience that already knew the wharf was losing money. The developer's brochure had a simple pitch: pretty condos, tax revenue, and maybe a culvert that finally gets fixed. Osgood could not win by pretending those numbers away. Instead she builds her speech like one of her channel crossings, carefully and in order. First she earns trust as a practical insider who admits the wharf's weaknesses. Then she redefines the wharf from a failing business into infrastructure the town cannot function without. Finally she shifts the question from money to who is actually on the water when something goes wrong. By the end, a vote that looked like a budget decision feels like a decision about what kind of town Tillet's Reach wants to be.

Osgood opens by shrinking her own authority in a way that actually increases it. "I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. I am a woman who knows where the rocks are." Listing what she is not lets her step out of the expert argument the council expects, and the plain image of the rocks suggests she knows dangers the planners don't. For an audience of neighbors, someone who climbed "a rope ladder" for thirty-one years is probably more trustworthy than a developer from out of town. Then, instead of mocking the brochure, she compliments it: "It is handsome." She never attacks the developers at all. She uses their own drawing as evidence, pointing out that it shows "not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot." The brochure's silence becomes her strongest exhibit, because the audience can see for themselves what the plan leaves out.

The most important move comes in paragraph 3, where Osgood concedes the facts the other side would use against her. The ice house closed, the fuel dock "loses money three months a year," and the town "cannot fix the culvert on Pell Street." By saying these things first, she takes them away from her opponents and shows the council members who want the tax money that she is not just being nostalgic. That concession is what makes the kitchen metaphor work: "It is not a gold mine. It is a kitchen." Nobody judges a kitchen by whether it turns a profit by itself; they judge it by whether the restaurant can run without it. The metaphor changes the standard the wharf is measured by. She then shows the consequences as a chain: "Then the mechanic goes. Then the welder." The sentences get shorter as the town loses more, so the losses fall like dominoes, ending with the kids who leave. And because she already admitted the bad numbers, the good ones, "four million dollars" and "one hundred and forty jobs," sound like honest counts and not a sales pitch.

Osgood saves the Anna Belle story for after the economics, and the placement is deliberate. She even flags the shift, calling it "something now that is harder to put in a brochure." Once the council has heard that the wharf is worth money, she shows that its real value can't be counted. Dale Cuttery reached the trawler in eleven minutes "because they were already there." Then come two blunt sentences: "It cannot. Nobody is aboard." The image of empty shrink-wrapped sailboats quietly turns the debate from profit to safety, and from what the waterfront looks like to who is physically present on it. It is hard to argue for a boardwalk after that without sounding like you'd trade a rescue for a view.

Finally, Osgood returns to where she started. "I have brought a great many ships safely in" sets up her wish "to help bring one town in too." The piloting metaphor ties the ethos of her opening to her request, so she sounds less like an opponent of progress and more like a guide through a dangerous channel. Even her last line, "let us sit down and find another way to pay for the culvert," keeps the concession alive, so nobody in the room has to choose between the wharf and the culvert. Osgood persuades because she never asks the town to ignore its problems. She only asks it to see what the brochure left out.

In her speech to the town meeting, Marguerite Osgood tries to convince the council to vote down the rezoning by presenting herself as a practical person who knows the harbor, and then by redefining the north wharf as something the whole town needs instead of just a business that is losing money. Osgood begins by building her credibility. She says "I am not a planner, a developer, or an economist. I am a woman who knows where the rocks are." By listing what she is not, she sounds humble and not like someone with an agenda, and the line about the rocks makes her sound like she has real experience. This matters because the audience is about to vote on a developer's plan, and she needs them to trust her over a glossy brochure. She also describes the brochure's pictures as having "not a single forklift, fuel barge, or crab pot," which points out what the developer left out and makes the audience notice what would be lost.

Next, Osgood makes a concession. She admits "The fishing fleet is smaller than it was" and that the ice house closed, and she says condominium taxes are "real money." This helps her because the people who want the tax money will not feel attacked, and it makes her seem fair and honest. Then she uses her metaphor: "It is not a gold mine. It is a kitchen." The kitchen idea works because everyone understands that a restaurant needs a kitchen even if the kitchen does not make money by itself. She then lists the mechanic, the welder, and the net patcher, and says "half of you" buy boots at the supply store, which speaks directly to the people in the room. The statistics about four million dollars and one hundred and forty jobs back this up and show the wharf is important to the economy.

The most powerful part is probably the Anna Belle story. Osgood changes her tone to say "something now that is harder to put in a brochure," and tells how Dale Cuttery got to the trawler in eleven minutes. Her short sentences, "It cannot. Nobody is aboard," make the point very clearly. This shows the wharf is also about safety and not only about money, which is something the condominiums can't replace.

Finally, she asks "what are we really deciding?" and says the waterfront will either "belong to the town or merely faces it." Her ending goes back to her piloting job by saying she wants to "bring one town in too," and she offers to help find another way to pay for the culvert. The Chair That Wobbles
Odalys Vreeland, column in the Kettle Hill Quarterly (fictional), 2026

When the school board in Pellingham voted last spring to require every student to complete a year of a hand craft before graduating, woodworking, weaving, bookbinding, bicycle repair, whatever the shop could staff, the objections came fast. Parents asked why a teenager who will never cut a dovetail joint should spend ninety hours learning to.
