parts.model_answer:
In eighth grade I glued up a maple cutting board with the grain running the wrong way, and three weeks later it split down the middle on my mom's counter. Nobody had to grade it. The board graded itself. I thought about that board while reading about the parents in Pellingham, because they are right that a machine could have made a better one in a minute. But they are missing what the crack taught me. Schools should require a hand craft, but only if it is taught as practice in living with mistakes that cannot be undone, not as a weak copy of factory training, and only if students get to choose the craft and the requirement is shorter than a full year.

The parents' best argument is about time, and it deserves a real answer. My friend Marcus wants to study computer science, and ninety more hours of coding would probably get him one more finished project for his portfolio. That matters. But the thing that makes coding easy to practice is also what limits it as a teacher. When Marcus breaks his program he hits Ctrl-Z or goes back to an earlier version, and the mistake disappears like it never happened. When I made my second board I measured three times before every cut, not because Mr. Halloran told me to, but because I had already watched one split. Coding and statistics teach students to be correct eventually. They are worse at teaching students to be careful beforehand, because they forgive too easily. A craft class gives Marcus something his other ninety hours can't.

It is also not true that manual judgment has vanished just because machines exist. The mechanic at the bike shop near my house trues wheels by spinning them and plucking the spokes like guitar strings, listening for the one that sounds flat. The shop owns a truing stand that measures automatically, but he told me it "doesn't know when the rim itself is bent." What he has isn't really speed or precision, since the machine beats him at both. What he has is the habit of noticing. That is why I think both sides in Pellingham are measuring the wrong thing when they talk about the chair. The parents treat the wobbling chair as a failure because a factory chair is better. But a factory chair can't tell you anything about the person who made it, and a wobbling chair is a record of exactly where the student's attention slipped. The point of the class is the wobble.

The parents also assume that school time is a fixed budget that should be spent on what students will "actually need." The problem is that nobody is very good at predicting that. My grandmother's high school required shorthand because every office supposedly needed it, and twenty years later the skill was useless. Some of the coding languages being pushed today may be written mostly by AI before current juniors finish college. If schools can't guess which skills will last, it makes more sense to spend some time on habits that carry over, like patience and taking responsibility for your own mistakes, than to spend every hour betting on the job market.

Still, there is a tension inside my own position. Part of why my cutting board meant something is that I wanted it to turn out well. A student forced into weaving who doesn't care will just put in the hours, and a box-checking requirement could kill the exact attention it is supposed to build. That is why the conditions matter. Students should pick their own craft, the class should be one semester, and grading should reward the reflection on what went wrong, not a polished final product. Pellingham's board chair said the requirement "is not about chairs." She's right, but the school has to actually teach it that way, or the parents will be right too.

I think schools should require a hand craft, but only for a limited amount of time and only if it is taught as a way of solving problems and not as job training. A full year of ninety hours for everybody is probably too much, but a semester that counts toward electives the students already have would be worth it.

The main reason is that making something by hand teaches you to deal with mistakes. In eighth grade I took a shop class where we had to build a small wooden toolbox. I measured one side wrong and cut it too short, and there was no undo button. I had to either start over with new wood or figure out a way to fix it, and I ended up adding a strip of wood to the bottom that made the box look kind of strange. The box was not good, but I remember what I learned from it. When you cannot delete a mistake you have to think about it before you do it. That is the same thing the board's chair meant when she said the requirement is not about chairs. A student who learns that carefulness in a shop might use it later when writing a paper or doing a lab, even if she never touches a saw again.

The parents have a point, though, that ninety hours is ninety hours. A student who wants to be an engineer might get more out of coding or statistics. That shows that even in a world of machines some jobs still need hands. defensible_positions: Schools should require a hand craft because it is the only school experience in which mistakes are physical and irreversible, and that experience cannot be replaced by any screen-based course.
Schools should not require a hand craft; the opportunity cost is real, students who want craft can elect it, and a requirement turns a pleasure into a chore.
A craft requirement is justified only if it is designed as training in judgment and recovery from error rather than as job preparation, and it should replace, not add to, existing requirements.

The requirement should exist precisely because machines are better: when output no longer matters, the only remaining reason to make something is what making does to the maker, and schools are the one place that reason can be protected.

Requiring a craft is less important than requiring some activity with real consequences, whether that is craft, cooking, caring for an animal, or repairing a machine; the specific demand for hand work is nostalgic.
The requirement is defensible but should come early (middle school) rather than in the final high school years when the tradeoff with academic courses is sharpest.
lines_of_reasoning: Consequence argument: nearly all school work can be undone or redone; a cut board cannot. Learning to live with and repair an irreversible mistake is a distinct kind of education, so the requirement buys something no other course provides. Evidence: a specific botched project and what the writer did next.

Opportunity-cost argument: ninety hours is a meaningful share of a school year; the student who needs statistics for a scholarship or a language for family reasons pays a real price. Electives already exist for those who want craft. Evidence: a concrete account of what a named course did for the writer or a classmate.

Automation-reversal argument: the parents' premise (the machine does it better, so why learn it) proves too much, since machines also compute, translate, and write. If usefulness were the test, most of the curriculum would go. So the test must be something else, and craft passes it. Evidence: an observed case where the ability to do a thing by hand changed how someone understood the machine version.

Requirement-undermines-value argument: the good of craft lies in attention and choice; compelled attention is not the same thing. A requirement produces students who resent the lathe. Evidence: contrast between a required class the writer endured and a chosen activity that actually taught something.

Equity argument: the students most likely to opt out of craft are exactly those who have never been near a workshop and whose families cannot supply the experience at home; a requirement is the only way they encounter it. Counter-consideration: those same students may most need the academic hours.

Reframing argument: the real question is what schools are for. If they exist to sort students into future jobs, the parents are right; if they exist to produce people who can act in the world, the board is right. The essay commits to one purpose and derives its position from it.

rhetorical_choices.device: concrete sensory detail in the board chair's question
rhetorical_choices.effect: Shifts the debate from economic usefulness to lived experience; a strong essay may notice that this move is persuasive but does not answer the opportunity-cost objection.

rhetorical_choices.device: repetition of 'ninety hours' as a fixed, transferable quantity
rhetorical_choices.effect: Frames school time as a budget; a sophisticated essay may challenge this framing rather than accept it.

source_uses.usable_for: Framing only. Writers may borrow the two competing claims (what a person loses by never making anything; what ninety hours could otherwise buy) as the tension their essay must resolve, but should supply their own evidence rather than retelling the Pellingham dispute.

common_pitfalls: Treating the prompt as 'are hand crafts good?' instead of 'should schools require them, and to what extent?' The requirement question involves tradeoffs that a general praise of craftsmanship ignores.
Summarizing or paraphrasing the Pellingham dispute as if it were evidence. The stimulus frames the issue; it does not supply proof.
Asserting that working with one's hands 'builds character' or 'teaches patience' without a single concrete example of how.
Inventing statistics or vague 'studies show' claims about automation or job markets.
Naming the opportunity-cost objection (ninety hours not spent elsewhere) and then moving on without answering it.
Equating hand craft with vocational training and arguing only about future employment, which misses the board chair's claim that the requirement 'is not about chairs'.
Taking a vague middle position ('it depends on the student') without specifying what it depends on or what the school should actually do.
Arguing that automation makes all manual skill worthless, or that automation is a myth, rather than engaging what actually changes when machines can do the task better.

samples.essay:
In eighth grade I glued up a maple cutting board with the grain running the wrong way, and three weeks later it split down the middle on my mom's counter. Nobody had to grade it. The board graded itself. I thought about that board while reading about the parents in Pellingham, because they are right that a machine could have made a better one in a minute. But they are missing what the crack taught me. Schools should require a hand craft, but only if it is taught as practice in living with mistakes that cannot be undone, not as a weak copy of factory training, and only if students get to choose the craft and the requirement is shorter than a full year.

The parents' best argument is about time, and it deserves a real answer. My friend Marcus wants to study computer science, and ninety more hours of coding would probably get him one more finished project for his portfolio. That matters. But the thing that makes coding easy to practice is also what limits it as a teacher. When Marcus breaks his program he hits Ctrl-Z or goes back to an earlier version, and the mistake disappears like it never happened. When I made my second board I measured three times before every cut, not because Mr. Halloran told me to, but because I had already watched one split. Coding and statistics teach students to be correct eventually. They are worse at teaching students to be careful beforehand, because they forgive too easily. A craft class gives Marcus something his other ninety hours can't.

It is also not true that manual judgment has vanished just because machines exist. The mechanic at the bike shop near my house trues wheels by spinning them and plucking the spokes like guitar strings, listening for the one that sounds flat. The shop owns a truing stand that measures automatically, but he told me it "doesn't know when the rim itself is bent." What he has isn't really speed or precision, since the machine beats him at both. What he has is the habit of noticing. That is why I think both sides in Pellingham are measuring the wrong thing when they talk about the chair. The parents treat the wobbling chair as a failure because a factory chair is better. But a factory chair can't tell you anything about the person who made it, and a wobbling chair is a record of exactly where the student's attention slipped. The point of the class is the wobble.

The parents also assume that school time is a fixed budget that should be spent on what students will "actually need." The problem is that nobody is very good at predicting that. My grandmother's high school required shorthand because every office supposedly needed it, and twenty years later the skill was useless. Some of the coding languages being pushed today may be written mostly by AI before current juniors finish college. If schools can't guess which skills will last, it makes more sense to spend some time on habits that carry over, like patience and taking responsibility for your own mistakes, than to spend every hour betting on the job market.

Still, there is a tension inside my own position. Part of why my cutting board meant something is that I wanted it to turn out well. A student forced into weaving who doesn't care will just put in the hours, and a box-checking requirement could kill the exact attention it is supposed to build. That is why the conditions matter. Students should pick their own craft, the class should be one semester, and grading should reward the reflection on what went wrong, not a polished final product. Pellingham's board chair said the requirement "is not about chairs." She's right, but the school has to actually teach it that way, or the parents will be right too.

It also sets the conditions the essay will argue for later: craft taught as meeting consequences, student choice, a shorter term. Someone could reasonably disagree with it, so it earns the point.

samples.essay:
I think schools should require a hand craft, but only for a limited amount of time and only if it is taught as a way of solving problems and not as job training. A full year of ninety hours for everybody is probably too much, but a semester that counts toward electives the students already have would be worth it.

The main reason is that making something by hand teaches you to deal with mistakes. In eighth grade I took a shop class where we had to build a small wooden toolbox. I measured one side wrong and cut it too short, and there was no undo button. I had to either start over with new wood or figure out a way to fix it, and I ended up adding a strip of wood to the bottom that made the box look kind of strange. The box was not good, but I remember what I learned from it. When you cannot delete a mistake you have to think about it before you do it. That is the same thing the board's chair meant when she said the requirement is not about chairs. A student who learns that carefulness in a shop might use it later when writing a paper or doing a lab, even if she never touches a saw again.

The parents have a point, though, that ninety hours is ninety hours. A student who wants to be an engineer might get more out of coding or statistics. But I think this objection assumes that school time is only for things that will be directly useful later. My uncle works as a mechanic and he says that the computers in cars can tell you what is wrong, but you still need to know how it feels when a bolt is about to strip. That shows that even in a world of machines some jobs still need hands. Also, nobody really knows which skills students will actually need, so a school that only teaches what looks useful now could be making a bad guess.

For this reason I would not make the requirement a full year. Machines really do make better chairs, so the point should not be the finished product. If the class is a semester and the students can pick which craft they do, then the cost is smaller and the benefit is still there. Students who choose bicycle repair or weaving will care more about it than students who are just forced into woodworking.

In conclusion, schools should require a short hand craft course because it teaches students to live with their mistakes, but they should keep it limited so it does not take too much time from other subjects.

annotations.comment: Specific observation about manual judgment in a workplace, but it is secondhand and only loosely connected to why all students should be required to take a craft.

annotations.comment: Gestures at the unreliability of predicting future needs, a possible sophisticated move, but it is a single unsupported sentence and not sustained.

samples.essay:
In Pellingham the school board wants every student to learn a hand craft before they graduate and some parents do not like it. I think there are good points on both sides of this issue and schools should think about it carefully.

On one hand, learning a craft is good for students. Working with your hands teaches you things that you cant learn from a book or a screen. Everyone knows that making something builds character and makes people more patient. The board chair said it is not about chairs and I agree with that. Even if a machine can make a better chair, a student who makes one will feel proud of it.

On the other hand, ninety hours is a lot of time. Students need to be ready for the future and the future is technology. Coding and statistics are things that jobs will need, so some parents are right to be worried. Machines do most of the work now anyway so a lot of people will never need to cut wood or sew.

In my own experience I took a shop class in ninth grade and we made a small birdhouse. Mine was not very good but I still liked it. It was fun to do something different from regular classes.

In conclusion, hand crafts can be valuable but so can other subjects. Schools should decide what is best for their students and balance the two things. There are many opinions about this topic but in the end education is about learning and both skills matter.

annotations.quote: I think there are good points on both sides of this issue and schools should think about it carefully.
annotations.comment: No defensible position on the requirement. This only says the issue has two sides and should be considered carefully, which earns no thesis credit.

annotations.quote: Schools should decide what is best for their students and balance the two things.
annotations.comment: The conclusion repeats the non-committal stance. It never says how far a craft requirement should go or under what conditions, so a reader has nothing to disagree with.

annotations.quote: Everyone knows that making something builds character and makes people more patient.
annotations.comment: General assertion with no concrete example. The claim is praise of craft in the abstract and is not tied to the requirement question.

annotations.quote: I took a shop class in ninth grade and we made a small birdhouse.
annotations.comment: This is the only specific evidence, but the commentary stops at 'it was fun.' It never explains what the birdhouse shows about whether every student should be required to do this.

annotations.quote: Coding and statistics are things that jobs will need, so some parents are right to be worried.
annotations.comment: The ninety-hours objection is named and mostly repeats the stimulus. The essay does not weigh what those hours would buy against what craft offers, so the central tension goes unanswered.

annotations.quote: There are many opinions about this topic but in the end education is about learning and both skills matter.
annotations.comment: This is a generic gesture at both sides within a mechanical intro, body and conclusion structure. It questions no assumption, such as time being a fixed quantity or usefulness being the measure, so there is no sophistication.

blueprint.issue: whether, and to what extent, schools should require every student to learn a hand craft when machines can perform most manual tasks better
stances: full endorsement of a universal requirement
full rejection in favor of electives
qualified endorsement conditioned on purpose, timing, or replacement of other requirements
